sections.skill: Identify the key terms of a contract and the questions to ask before signing

questions.prompt: Jamal is about to sign a gym membership contract. Which part tells him how to end it?

choices.text: The gym's logo and address at the top of the page
The list of classes offered this month
The photo on his membership card

questions.intro: A contract is a legally binding agreement. Key parts: the parties, what each promises, the price and fees, the length (term), how it renews, how to cancel, and how disputes are handled. Read every page before signing and keep a copy.
questions.feedback: Cancellation terms explain how and when the contract can be ended and at what cost.

misconceptions.C: Not part of the contract terms

sources: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs: New Jersey residents can file consumer complaints, including about contracts and refund policies, with the Division of Consumer Affairs. (https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/)

questions.prompt: The gym contract is $35 a month for 12 months, plus a $49 sign-up fee and a $60 annual fee. What is the first-year cost?
questions.intro: The full cost of a contract includes monthly charges plus one-time and yearly fees.
sources: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs: New Jersey residents can file consumer complaints, including about contracts and refund policies, with the Division of Consumer Affairs. (https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/)

questions.prompt: A salesperson says, "Don't worry about the fine print; you can cancel anytime." The written contract says cancellation costs $150. Which usually controls?

choices.text: The salesperson's spoken promise, because it came first
Neither, since gym contracts are not binding

questions.intro: If a promise matters, get it in writing in the contract. Signed written terms usually control over spoken promises.
questions.feedback: Signed written terms usually control; ask for promises in writing.

misconceptions.A: Spoken promises are hard to prove

sources: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs: New Jersey residents can file consumer complaints, including about contracts and refund policies, with the Division of Consumer Affairs. (https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/)

questions.prompt: The contract says disputes go to "binding arbitration." What does that usually mean?

choices.text: Jamal can sue in any court he chooses
The gym must refund him automatically
A private arbitrator decides instead of a court
A judge must approve every monthly bill the gym sends

questions.correct_answer: A private arbitrator decides instead of a court
questions.intro: An arbitration clause sends disputes to a private arbitrator, often limiting class actions and appeals.
questions.feedback: Arbitration replaces a court case with a private decision.
sources: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs: New Jersey residents can file consumer complaints, including about contracts and refund policies, with the Division of Consumer Affairs. (https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/)

questions.prompt: Jamal is 17. In most states, what is generally true of contracts signed by minors?

choices.text: They are stricter than adult contracts
The minor can often cancel them
They can never be signed at all

questions.correct_answer: The minor can often cancel them
questions.intro: In most states, including New Jersey, the age of majority is 18. Many contracts signed by minors are voidable by the minor, though contracts for necessities can be enforced. Businesses often require a parent to cosign.
questions.feedback: Minors can usually void many contracts, which is why businesses ask for a parent's signature.

questions.prompt: After canceling, the gym keeps charging Jamal's debit card. What should he do first?

choices.text: Ignore it and hope it stops
Stop opening his bank statements until it ends
Contact his bank and dispute the charges
Pay extra to make them stop

questions.correct_answer: Contact his bank and dispute the charges
questions.intro: Banks can stop recurring payments and investigate unauthorized charges. Keep the cancellation proof.
questions.feedback: The bank can block and investigate charges; New Jersey residents can also complain to the Division of Consumer Affairs.
